episodes.theme: Documented record + legend: the Oak Island Money Pit (Oak Island, Mahone Bay, Nova Scotia, Canada). Legend (first printed 1850s-60s): 1795 Daniel McGinnis found a round saucer-shaped dip; with John Smith and Anthony Vaughan dug: flagstones ~2 ft, log layers, stopped ~30 ft. Truro Company 1849: drill at ~98 ft through wood, 'metal in pieces'; water rose and fell with the tide -> flood-tunnel theory. 1909 Franklin D. Roosevelt in Old Gold Salvage, followed it all his life. 1931 Chappell: axe, anchor, miner's pick at ~127 ft. Woods Hole 1995: flooding natural (fresh-water lens + tides); geologists: sinkhole/caves. No treasure ever confirmed. Deaths/curse deliberately left out.

Large black spaniel with curly shaggy hair; came out of a passage (through the old church to the Captain of the Guard's rooms) at dusk, lay by the guard-room fire when candles were lit, went back at dawn. Soldiers got used to it but would not swear near it or be alone with it; keys carried in pairs. A drunk soldier took the keys alone; a loud noise was heard; he came back sober and silent and never told what he saw (his death three days later left out). Passage closed, dog never seen in the castle again. Walter Scott used it in Peveril of the Peak (1823).

In 1662 (Glanvill dates it March 1661) John Mompesson had the vagrant drummer William Drury arrested at Ludgershall for a forged pass; Drury was freed but his drum was taken and later sent to Mompesson's house. Nightly knocking and drumming followed, on the roof and in the room with the drum, starting when the lights went out; it stopped three weeks after Mrs Mompesson gave birth, then returned, shaking the children's beds. Mompesson's letter of 6 Dec 1662 mentions a 'supernatural beating of drums'; Joseph Glanvill visited in Jan 1663, heard scratching in the girls' room and found nothing; published in Saducismus Triumphatus (1681). Drury reportedly bragged in prison ('I have plagued him...'); tried for witchcraft at Salisbury 1663, not found guilty. Hoax was suspected; never proved.

One Saturday night in October 1817, Edmund Lenthal Swifte, Keeper of the Crown Jewels, sat at supper in the Jewel House with his wife, their little son and her sister. uploads.description:
He stepped outside to the horses. A few seconds later he was gone. This is a true story.

On 25 November 1809, in the small town of Perleberg in Prussia, Benjamin Bathurst, a 25-year-old British diplomat, was hurrying home to England from Vienna during the Napoleonic wars. He travelled under a false name, as a merchant called Koch, and believed enemy agents were following him. He waited for fresh horses at the White Swan inn. At about nine o'clock the carriage was ready. Bathurst stepped outside and walked toward the horses, his courier Krause a few steps behind him, and he was never seen again. The river was dragged and the town searched house by house; his fur coat turned up in an outhouse. On 16 December two old women gathering sticks in the woods near Quitzow found his grey trousers, turned inside out, with two bullet holes but no blood, and a half-finished letter to his wife in the pocket. His wife Phillida travelled to Germany to search for him. He was never found.

He walked round the tomb twelve times. Then thirteen. Then he put his finger in the keyhole. This is a true legend.

In the churchyard of Holy Trinity, on the hill above Buckfastleigh in Devon, England, stands a small stone house with iron bars: the tomb of Squire Richard Cabell of Brook Manor, who died on 5 July 1677. People said he was a cruel hunter who had sold his soul. The legend says that on the night of his burial a pack of black hounds came racing across Dartmoor to howl at his grave, and that every year he rides out again with his phantom pack. The townspeople laid a heavy stone over him and built the tomb house around it so he could not get out. Children dared each other to walk round it thirteen (some say seven) times and put a finger in the keyhole. In 1901 Arthur Conan Doyle came to Dartmoor and heard these stories; soon after he wrote The Hound of the Baskervilles. The old church burned in 1992. The tomb still stands.

A figure scratched at her window, picked away the lead around one small pane, reached in, turned the catch and came in. Her brothers drove it off and it fled over the wall into the churchyard. In the morning every coffin was broken open except one, and in it lay a dried brown figure with a fresh wound in its leg. So the story says, they burned it. Hare printed the tale in his Story of My Life (1896-1900). In 1924 the writer Charles G. Harper went looking and found no Croglin Grange, and the church has no record of a family vault.
